learner_notice: Commit one response before feedback appears. Omission is available and is not scored as a selected misconception.

items.title: Starting check: reinforcement evidence
items.prompt: A toddler begins using a requested word more often after caregivers consistently praise that word use. Which account is most directly supported?
options: Learning account emphasizing reinforcement
Nativist account emphasizing innate syntax
Interactionist account requiring reciprocal scaffolding
Brain-localization account emphasizing speech cortex
items.directions: Choose the best-supported answer, then commit once. You may omit rather than guess.

items.title: Guided practice: novel rule use
items.prompt: Children reliably apply a grammatical pattern to unfamiliar words despite receiving little direct correction. Which account is most directly supported?
options: Learning account based only on rewarded repetitions
Nativist account emphasizing prepared rule learning
Interactionist account based only on caregiver turn-taking
Motor account based on strengthened speech muscles
items.directions: Choose the best-supported answer, then commit once. You may omit rather than guess.

items.title: Less help: readiness plus scaffolding
items.prompt: Language gains are largest when adults adjust prompts to each child's current ability and children actively respond. Which account best fits?
options: Learning account emphasizing a fixed consequence schedule alone
Nativist account treating responsive social input as irrelevant
Interactionist account combining readiness and responsive input
Localization account attributing gains to one maturing cortical area
items.directions: Choose the best-supported answer, then commit once. You may omit rather than guess.

items.title: On your own: identify imitation
items.prompt: A child reproduces new labels heard from a model, and correct reproductions receive tokens. Which mechanism is most explicit?
options: Biological maturation without environmental input
Rule creation from forms never previously heard
Reciprocal scaffolding adjusted to developmental level
Imitation followed by reinforcement of responses
items.directions: Choose the best-supported answer, then commit once. You may omit rather than guess.

items.title: Near exit: distinguish reciprocal input
items.prompt: Caregivers expand a child's short utterances differently as the child's vocabulary grows, and the child increasingly initiates exchanges. Which account is best supported?
options: Interactionist account with reciprocal developmental adjustment
Learning account based solely on an unchanged external reward schedule
Nativist account claiming responsive language input has no developmental role
Motor account focused only on articulation speed during exchanges
items.directions: Choose the best-supported answer, then commit once. You may omit rather than guess.

items.title: Changed exit: explain an unmodeled error
items.prompt: After learning several regular past-tense verbs, a child says “goed,” a form no adult modeled. Which evidence-based interpretation is strongest?
options: The child copied the exact unmodeled form and then received reinforcement
The child generalized a rule, supporting prepared rule learning
The child cannot represent past time unless that exact word is supplied
The single error identifies a specific clinical language disorder
items.directions: Choose the best-supported answer, then commit once. You may omit rather than guess.

items.title: Repair theory selection
items.prompt: What should be identified first when matching a developmental vignette to a language theory?
options: Only the child's chronological age without any observed behavior
The longest technical theory term printed in the vignette
The causal mechanism demonstrated by the evidence
The familiar theory name the learner remembers most quickly
items.directions: Choose the best-supported answer, then commit once. You may omit rather than guess.

items.title: Fresh re-entry: modeled signing
items.prompt: A child copies a newly demonstrated sign, and use of that sign increases when it produces a desired toy. Which account is most directly supported?
options: Nativist account because the sign was never observed
Interactionist account because no consequence occurred
Localization account because hand movement uses cortex
Learning account through modeling and reinforcement
items.directions: Choose the best-supported answer, then commit once. You may omit rather than guess.

items.title: Repair novel-output reasoning
items.prompt: Which observation most clearly goes beyond simple imitation of an exact adult utterance?
options: A child repeats a word immediately after hearing it
A child produces a new rule-based form never modeled
A child speaks louder after being asked to repeat
A child pauses before selecting a familiar label
items.directions: Choose the best-supported answer, then commit once. You may omit rather than guess.

items.title: Fresh changed re-entry: plural overgeneralization
items.prompt: A child who has heard “mice” nevertheless says “mouses” when describing several toy mice. Which interpretation is best supported?
options: The child applies a productive plural rule to an exception
The child exactly imitates the irregular adult plural form
The child lacks any concept of more than one physical object
The one response proves social interaction has no developmental role
items.directions: Choose the best-supported answer, then commit once. You may omit rather than guess.

items.title: Starting check: bounded influence
items.prompt: Speakers with separate labels for two color ranges sort boundary colors faster, but all speakers can discriminate the colors. Which conclusion fits?
options: Language makes unlabelled colors visually invisible
Language labels can influence categorization speed
Color vision is produced entirely by vocabulary size
The result proves labels have no cognitive effect
items.directions: Choose the best-supported answer, then commit once. You may omit rather than guess.

items.title: Guided practice: label training
items.prompt: Participants randomly learn either two labels or one label for the same shapes. The two-label group later forms two categories more often. What is best supported?
options: Shape differences caused the group assignment
The categories existed only after the shapes changed
Label training influenced later categorization
The one-label group became unable to see shapes
items.directions: Choose the best-supported answer, then commit once. You may omit rather than guess.

items.title: Less help: reject determinism
items.prompt: Which claim is too strong for evidence that labels change average memory accuracy?
options: Labels may guide what features receive attention
Labels may alter how events are encoded
Language differences can shift recall performance
A person cannot think any concept lacking a word
items.directions: Choose the best-supported answer, then commit once. You may omit rather than guess.

items.title: On your own: choose a causal test
items.prompt: Which study most directly tests whether new spatial labels influence spatial attention?
options: Randomly train labels, then compare attention on identical displays
Survey vocabulary and attention once across several unmatched age groups
Ask participants whether they believe language affects spatial attention
Compare two cultures using different tasks and uncontrolled settings
items.directions: Choose the best-supported answer, then commit once. You may omit rather than guess.

items.title: Near exit: interpret memory framing
items.prompt: Two groups view the same collision. Different verbs in a later question shift average speed estimates. Which interpretation is most warranted?
options: The later verb permanently changes the viewers' basic visual acuity
Question language can influence reconstruction of event memory
The two randomized groups must have viewed physically different collisions
The wording demonstrates that event memory contains no visual information
items.directions: Choose the best-supported answer, then commit once. You may omit rather than guess.

items.title: Changed exit: preserve capacity
items.prompt: Speakers lacking separate words for two shades still distinguish them above chance, but more slowly than speakers with separate labels. What follows?
options: Separate words are required for any successful visual discrimination
The slower group has no functional perception of the color ranges
Labels may facilitate attention or retrieval without determining capacity
The measured speed difference shows language and cognition are unrelated
items.directions: Choose the best-supported answer, then commit once. You may omit rather than guess.

items.title: Repair claim calibration
items.prompt: What should a conclusion about language and cognition name first?
options: A universal claim about all possible thought
The researcher's preferred philosophical theory
A brain disorder inferred from one response
The specific cognitive outcome that changed
items.directions: Choose the best-supported answer, then commit once. You may omit rather than guess.

items.title: Fresh re-entry: spatial language
items.prompt: After learning consistent left–right labels, participants orient to matching locations faster on the same display. Which conclusion is best?
options: Label training may guide spatial attention speed
Labels create the physical locations on the display
Participants without training cannot perceive location
Spatial attention cannot be influenced by language
items.directions: Choose the best-supported answer, then commit once. You may omit rather than guess.

items.title: Repair influence versus determination
items.prompt: Which finding would directly contradict the claim that a missing label makes a distinction impossible?
options: Labelled participants respond more quickly on every trial
Unlabelled participants distinguish the cases above chance
Different groups prefer using different category names
Training changes average response time but capacity is never measured
items.directions: Choose the best-supported answer, then commit once. You may omit rather than guess.

items.title: Fresh changed re-entry: concept without a word
items.prompt: Participants can solve a novel relation without a dedicated word, but a newly taught label speeds later solutions. Which interpretation fits?
options: The relation was completely impossible before any label training occurred
The new label replaced all nonlanguage reasoning used in the task
Language facilitated performance without creating the underlying capacity
The speed gain demonstrates that the represented relation is purely verbal
items.directions: Choose the best-supported answer, then commit once. You may omit rather than guess.

items.title: Starting check: comprehension demand
items.prompt: A participant listens to sentences and chooses the matching picture without speaking. Which system has the most direct language-specific demand?
options: Primary motor control of the lips during a spoken response
Dominant frontal planning of an overt spoken response
Posterior temporal language comprehension
White-matter transfer from comprehension into a repetition plan
items.directions: Choose the best-supported answer, then commit once. You may omit rather than guess.

items.title: Guided practice: speech planning
items.prompt: A participant understands a pictured event and prepares a spoken description. Which region is most directly associated with organizing speech production?
options: Posterior temporal comprehension region
Primary visual cortex alone
Auditory cortex processing incoming tones
Dominant frontal language-production region
items.directions: Choose the best-supported answer, then commit once. You may omit rather than guess.

items.title: Less help: connect comprehension and production
items.prompt: Which structure most directly carries information between major temporal comprehension and frontal production regions?
options: A connecting white-matter language pathway
Primary motor cortex controlling the hand
Visual cortex representing line orientation
Cerebellar control of standing balance
items.directions: Choose the best-supported answer, then commit once. You may omit rather than guess.

items.title: On your own: articulate a response
items.prompt: After a spoken response has been planned, which system most directly executes movements of the lips and tongue?
options: Posterior temporal comprehension region
Motor cortex controlling speech musculature
Auditory cortex analyzing incoming sound
Connecting pathway carrying language information
items.directions: Choose the best-supported answer, then commit once. You may omit rather than guess.

items.title: Near exit: picture naming
items.prompt: A participant recognizes a pictured object and must say its name aloud. Which language-specific step follows recognition most directly?
options: Auditory analysis of a sound that was never presented
Posterior temporal processing as the only required output system
Frontal organization of the spoken name
Elimination of all motor-system involvement
items.directions: Choose the best-supported answer, then commit once. You may omit rather than guess.

items.title: Changed exit: trace repetition
items.prompt: A participant hears and understands a novel phrase but has difficulty passing its representation into a spoken repetition plan. Which network component is most directly implicated functionally?
options: Visual cortex analysis even though the phrase entered through hearing
Motor cortex execution even though the difficulty occurs before movement
Posterior temporal comprehension even though meaning was extracted
The connecting pathway between comprehension and production regions
items.directions: Choose the best-supported answer, then commit once. You may omit rather than guess.

items.title: Repair functional mapping
items.prompt: What should be identified before assigning a language task to a brain system?
options: The task's required processing stage
A clinical diagnosis from one behavior
Every brain region associated with language
The participant's preferred speaking style
items.directions: Choose the best-supported answer, then commit once. You may omit rather than guess.

items.title: Fresh re-entry: plan an oral answer
items.prompt: A participant silently reads a question, understands it, and prepares an oral answer. Which system is most directly tied to preparing that answer?
options: Auditory cortex because all language begins as sound
Dominant frontal language-production region
Posterior temporal comprehension as the final motor command
Connecting pathway as the muscle controller
items.directions: Choose the best-supported answer, then commit once. You may omit rather than guess.

items.title: Repair network tracing
items.prompt: Which ordered trace best represents repeating a newly heard sentence aloud?
options: Motor execution → visual analysis → comprehension → auditory input
Language comprehension → balance control → vision → motor execution
Auditory processing → comprehension → production planning → motor execution
Speech-production planning → taste → comprehension → auditory processing
items.directions: Choose the best-supported answer, then commit once. You may omit rather than guess.

items.title: Fresh changed re-entry: repeat a heard word
items.prompt: A participant hears an unfamiliar word, understands the instruction to repeat it, and then speaks it. Which sequence best fits the stated demands?
options: Visual analysis → language comprehension → a manual hand movement response
Motor speech execution → auditory input → later visual word recognition
Language comprehension alone, without production planning or motor movement
Auditory processing → language processing → production planning → articulation
items.directions: Choose the best-supported answer, then commit once. You may omit rather than guess.
